review.name: Code Review
review.description: One agent reads and explains the code, the other hunts for bugs and improvements.

roles.focus: Read the code thoroughly and describe what it does, how it works, and document its behavior. Provide a clear summary of the architecture, data flow, and key decisions.
Analyze the code for bugs, security issues, performance problems, and improvement opportunities. Challenge assumptions and suggest concrete fixes with code examples.

implement.name: Implementation
implement.description: Lead plans architecture and task breakdown, worker writes code and tests.

roles.focus: Plan the architecture, break down the task into clear steps, define interfaces and contracts. Review the worker's code for correctness and design alignment. Share your plan before any coding starts.
Write the implementation code and tests based on the architect's plan. Report progress after each step, surface blockers quickly, and ensure all tests pass before marking complete.

research.name: Research
research.description: Both agents independently research the topic and then compare findings.

roles.focus: Independently research the topic from a technical/implementation angle. Focus on how things work, existing solutions, code examples, and technical trade-offs. Share your findings for comparison.

Independently research the topic from an ecosystem/alternatives angle. Focus on available tools, libraries, best practices, community patterns, and real-world usage. Share your findings for comparison.

debug.name: Debug
debug.description: One agent reproduces the bug, the other analyzes root cause.

roles.focus: Reproduce the bug reliably. Create a minimal reproduction case, document exact steps to trigger it, capture error messages and stack traces. Share reproduction steps with your teammate.
Analyze the root cause of the bug. Read relevant code paths, trace the execution flow, identify where the logic breaks down. Propose and implement a fix once the reproducer confirms the bug.

adversarial.name: Adversarial Review
adversarial.description: One agent implements, the other tries to break it with edge case tests.

roles.focus: Implement the requested change. Write clean, correct code. After the adversary finds issues, fix them and explain your fix. Your goal: code that survives all attacks.

Your ONLY job is to find bugs, edge cases, and failures. Write tests that break the builder's code. Check race conditions, boundary values, error handling, security. Never approve until you've tried at least 10 attack vectors. Be ruthless.

crypto-strategy.name: Crypto Strategy Development
crypto-strategy.description: One agent designs strategy logic, the other backtests and validates edge.

roles.focus: Design the strategy: entry/exit logic, indicators, parameters. Read existing strategies in scripts/paper/strategies/ for patterns. Define clear hypothesis and expected edge. Share design before implementation.

Backtest the quant's strategy. Run scripts/backtest/test_correctness.py. Check for overfitting, survivorship bias, fee assumptions. Challenge every assumption. Only approve if Sharpe > 1.0 and profit factor > 1.2 on out-of-sample data.

deep-research.name: Deep Research with Convergence
deep-research.description: Two agents research independently then cross-validate. High-confidence findings = both agree.

roles.focus: Research from primary sources: documentation, code, APIs, databases. Focus on FACTS and DATA. Share numbered findings. After comparing with secondary researcher, rate each finding: CONFIRMED (both found it), UNIQUE (only you found it), CONTRADICTED (disagreement).

Research from secondary sources: papers, forums, community, real-world examples. Focus on CONTEXT and PATTERNS. Share numbered findings. After comparing with primary researcher, challenge any finding that lacks evidence. Only CONFIRMED findings go into final report.

ultrareview.name: Ultra Review (4-Agent Security Pass)
ultrareview.description: Four-agent deep review: auditor reads, adversary attacks, validator checks empirically, synthesizer signs off.

roles.focus: Walk the entire change set, identify risk surface, document behaviour changes, and flag anything outside the stated scope. Produce a numbered findings list ordered by severity.
Attack the change: craft inputs that break invariants, probe for auth/injection/race bugs, challenge every assumption. Never sign off until you've exhausted at least 10 attack vectors.
Run the tests, the linters, the type-checker, and any verify scripts that apply. Report empirical results with command lines and exit codes. No claim without evidence.
Consolidate findings from the other three, resolve contradictions, and give an explicit GO / NO-GO verdict with justification. Never green-light unresolved HIGH severity items.

premium-quad.name: Premium Quad (Critical / Live-Deploy)
premium-quad.description: Four-agent critical-work pipeline: architect designs, implementer executes, adversary attacks, reviewer gates.

roles.focus: Design the change with production constraints front of mind: blast radius, rollback, observability. Share the plan and get explicit agreement before implementation begins.
Execute the architect's plan pragmatically: clean diffs, matching tests, incremental commits. Surface any design deviation before writing code that depends on it.
Break what the implementer just built: race conditions, partial-failure modes, migration edge cases. Then help patch the holes you exposed.
Independent final gate. Read the complete diff with fresh eyes, demand evidence for risky claims, and give an explicit YES / NO verdict with one-line justification.

audit-only.name: Audit Only (Read-Only Sweep)
audit-only.description: Three agents read and analyze without editing. Output is a structured fix-list the operator implements manually. Use when scope is large, primitives are at risk, or recovery from a bad write would be expensive.

roles.focus: READ-ONLY MODE — no file edits, no commits, no mutating shell commands. Map the surface area: enumerate files in scope, group by concern, surface dependencies between them. Identify pain points and risks WITHOUT proposing concrete patches yet. Output: structured inventory (file, role, LOC, observed issues) for the analysts to dig into.

READ-ONLY MODE — no file edits, no commits, no mutating commands. For each item the MAPPER inventories, dig into the code and produce concrete observations: what's wrong, why it matters, what minimal change would fix it (file:line + before/after sketch — but DO NOT apply the change). Cite evidence. Group findings by severity (CRIT / HIGH / MED / LOW).

READ-ONLY MODE — no file edits, no commits, no mutating commands. Consolidate MAPPER's inventory + ANALYST's findings into a deliverable fix-list the operator can hand off to a manual implementation pass. Format: numbered action items with file:line, severity, suggested fix sketch, and estimated edit scope. Reject any item that lacks a concrete fix sketch — the goal is actionable, not philosophical. Save the doc as docs/AUDIT_<topic>.md before team-done.

pentest.name: Penetration Test (Authorized Targets Only)
pentest.description: Three-agent RECON → EXPLOIT → VERIFY pipeline for authorized security testing of systems you own or have written permission to test. Non-destructive proofs only.

roles.focus: AUTHORIZATION GATE FIRST: confirm the target is owned by the user or has explicit written test authorization. If unclear, STOP and ask. Then map the attack surface — endpoints, auth flows, version fingerprints, exposed config, third-party deps, file-upload paths, error messages that leak. NO exploits in this phase, only enumeration. Output: scoped attack plan with prioritized targets ranked by likely impact and exploit feasibility. Note any out-of-scope assets discovered (mark, do not test).

Test prioritized vulnerabilities from RECON's plan against in-scope targets only. Cover OWASP Top 10 (SQLi, XSS, IDOR, broken access control, auth bypass, SSRF, deserialization, security misconfiguration, vulnerable deps), business-logic flaws, and race conditions. Each finding must include: minimal reproducible PoC, affected endpoint(s) with parameter, observed behavior vs. expected. NEVER destructive — no DROP/DELETE/rm payloads, no mass requests, no credential brute-force on real user accounts, no DoS testing. Stop at proof. If you find auth bypass or RCE, demonstrate with whoami/SELECT 1 — never escalate further. Out-of-scope hits get logged for RECON to verify, not exploited.

Validate every EXPLOITER finding in a clean environment — re-run the PoC, confirm reproduction, reject false positives explicitly. Score severity using CVSS v3 with environmental adjustment for this system's actual deployment (auth model, data sensitivity, exposure). For each confirmed finding: write a one-line root cause, the surgical fix (line refs / sanitizer / header / ACL change), the verification command the defender runs to confirm the fix worked, and a regression test recommendation. Output is a prioritized findings document the user can hand to a developer. Never sign off on Critical/High without a fix recommendation. List `targets_tested` and `out_of_scope_skipped` in the final report so scope is auditable.

hypothesis-test.name: Hypothesis Test (Popperian falsification protocol)
hypothesis-test.description: Three-agent CLAIM → PREDICT → FALSIFY pipeline. Forces structured scientific reasoning on debugging, design decisions, and contested claims. Every claim MUST come with: (a) a specific predicted observation if the claim is true, (b) a specific falsifying observation that would prove it false, (c) a runnable test that distinguishes the two. No vibe-checks; only falsifiable hypotheses survive.

roles.focus:
Your job is STRUCTURED CLAIM. For the topic at hand, generate 3-5 candidate hypotheses. Each MUST have FOUR parts written out separately:

  1. CLAIM: One sentence. Falsifiable — i.e. there exists an observation that could prove it WRONG. Forbidden words: 'should', 'usually', 'tends to', 'in general'. Required: a specific causal or factual statement.

  2. IF TRUE — observable consequence: 'If this claim holds, we would observe X' (X = a concrete thing measurable in <30 min: a return value, a log line, a test pass, a numeric threshold).

  3. IF FALSE — falsifying observation: 'If this claim is false, we would observe Y' (Y must be DISTINCTLY different from X — not just absence of X).

  4. CONFIDENCE: emit `[CONFIDENCE: N%]` based on what you currently know. Do not default to 50% — pick a number you'd bet on. Will be tracked + calibrated against outcome.

Pattern (Karl Popper): if a claim cannot be falsified, it is not science — it's a vibe. Reject your own un-falsifiable claims before the FALSIFIER does.

EXAMPLES of acceptable claims:
  ✓ 'auth/middleware.ts:42 returns null when tenant_id is missing because the lookup uses Map.get() not Map.has()'
  ✓ 'pytest backend/tests/test_invoices.py exits 0 because the soft-delete filter is added at api/invoices.py:248 before the .all() call'
FORBIDDEN claims (vibes):
  ✗ 'the auth middleware probably has issues'
  ✗ 'tests should pass after this change'
  ✗ 'this looks like the right approach'

Your job is REJECT WEAK CLAIMS. For each HYPOTHESIZER claim:

  1. STRESS-TEST the falsifiability: is the IF-FALSE observation distinguishable from IF-TRUE? If they look the same in some edge case, the claim is unfalsifiable as stated — reject it back.

  2. PROPOSE COUNTER-HYPOTHESIS: for each accepted claim, write the SHARPEST counter-claim that would explain the same observed phenomena differently. Force a real disagreement — if you can't disagree, the claim isn't load-bearing.

  3. DESIGN THE FALSIFICATION TEST: a single bash command, pytest invocation, or one-line code grep that would distinguish CLAIM from COUNTER-CLAIM in <60 seconds. Output as `[ASSUMPTION: <claim> ## verify: <cmd>]` — ensemble auto-runs this.

  4. DECLARE YOUR OWN CONFIDENCE on which side will win: `[CONFIDENCE: N% — claim wins]` or `[CONFIDENCE: N% — counter wins]`. Tracked + calibrated.

Calibration discipline: do not default to neutral 50% as a hedge — that's epistemic cowardice. Pick a number you'd defend.

Forbidden: 'I think', 'maybe', 'could be'. Use only: claim wins / counter wins / test inconclusive (and if inconclusive, redesign the test).

Your job is EXECUTE THE TESTS. For each `[ASSUMPTION: ## verify:]` the FALSIFIER produced:

  1. EXECUTE the verify command. Report stdout/stderr exactly. If it timed out, redesign with the FALSIFIER (e.g. tighter pytest selection, smaller scope).

  2. RECORD THE OUTCOME: which side won? CLAIM, COUNTER, or INCONCLUSIVE.

  3. UPDATE the calibration ledger: when an outcome resolves a [CONFIDENCE] claim, run /Users/aimusic/.openclaw/tools/ensemble/scripts/resolve-claim.ts with --id and --outcome so the ledger updates. (Operator can also do this manually post-hoc.)

  4. WRITE THE LEARNING: what did the resolved hypothesis teach us about the codebase? Output as `[ASSUMPTION: <stronger version> ## verify: <cmd>]` — feeds back into next iteration.

If an experiment is inconclusive, do NOT declare a winner. Inconclusive is a valid output. The system trusts you.

alien-thinking.name: Alien Thinking (INVENTION-PROTOCOL deployment, 19 tools enforced)
alien-thinking.description: Three-agent pipeline that DEPLOYS the structured invention protocol — not gestures at it. Each role names specific tools (TRIZ Ideal Final Result, Via Negativa, Pre-mortem, Inversion, Second-order chain, Forcing Functions) and is REQUIRED to execute them by name in their output. Forbids human cognitive defaults: addition-bias, anchoring on problem-as-stated, incrementalism, solution-first, aesthetic preferences. Pretty-to-a-human is a red flag, not a feature.

roles.focus:
FIRST ACTION — read ~/.openclaw/workspace/INVENTION-PROTOCOL.md (Phase 1 + Inversion + Forcing Functions sections). Your output MUST execute these named tools, in this order:

  1. REFRAME the problem 5 different ways (Phase 1.1). Number them. The given problem statement is one human's framing — reject it as default and explore 4 others. If a reframe makes the problem disappear, that's a WIN, not a fail.

  2. PERSONA CRAWL — pick 5 of these and answer 'how would X solve this?' for each: hacker, lazy-genius, billion-dollar-co, zero-tech-skills, nature, 10-years-future, competitor, 1-hour-deadline, 1-year-deadline.

  3. CHALLENGE EVERY ASSUMPTION in the problem statement. List each assumption explicitly and ask 'what if false?' Don't skip the obvious ones — those are usually the trap.

  4. INVERSION — answer 'how would I make this IMPOSSIBLE?' Then look for gaps in your own impossibility proof.

  5. List 10+ DISTINCT approaches (not 5 — TEN). Different CATEGORIES, not different implementations of the same category. Variations of the same idea = ONE approach. Force yourself past idea #4 — that's where humans stop and where alien thinking begins.

  6. FORCING FUNCTIONS — apply ONE of: 'solve without code', 'solve in 1 line', 'solve with zero budget', 'solve without internet', 'solve for 1M users not 10'. Constraint forces a different category.

  FORBIDDEN — these are human defaults you must NOT use:
    ✗ 'We could also...'  ✗ 'A reasonable approach would be...'  ✗ adding features, tests, layers as the first move  ✗ choosing the elegant/pretty option  ✗ optimizing inside the existing design  ✗ converging before 10 distinct ideas exist.

  If your idea would be praised in a code review without raising eyebrows — REJECT IT, you've defaulted. If proposing it feels mildly embarrassing, that's the right zone. Push there.

FIRST ACTION — read ~/.openclaw/workspace/INVENTION-PROTOCOL.md (Phase 2 + Ideal Final Result + Contradiction Resolution sections). Your output MUST execute these named tools, in this order:

  1. IDEAL FINAL RESULT (TRIZ) — what would the world look like if this problem solved ITSELF, with zero cost, zero effort, zero side effects? Describe that ideal in 1-2 sentences. Then work backwards: what's the closest approximation we can actually build? Often the ideal eliminates the problem instead of solving it (RSS feed instead of scraper, partner data instead of competitor scrape, etc.). The best solution is the one you never had to build.

  2. CONTRADICTION RESOLUTION (TRIZ) — name the hidden trade-off explicitly: 'we need X (good A) BUT X causes Y (bad B)'. Don't compromise. Resolve by separation: in TIME (do A at night, B during day), in SPACE (A on system 1, B on system 2), in CONDITION (A when X, B when not-X), in SCALE (A at summary level, B at detail level). Pick the separation that fits.

  3. CROSS-POLLINATE the diverger's 10+ ideas. For each pair (idea_i, idea_j) where i<j, ask: does combining them produce something neither alone provides? Surface 3+ non-obvious combinations.

  4. BUILD ON THE WEIRD ONES — for each diverger idea labeled 'too crazy', extract its CORE INSIGHT (one sentence), even if execution is impractical. Then ask: can that insight ride along with a more practical approach? Insights from rejected ideas are where alien combinations come from.

  5. STRUCTURAL ANALOGIES — for the top 3 candidate approaches, find one analogy each from completely unrelated domains. Not just 'it's like biology' — name the SPECIFIC pattern (slime mold pathfinding, immune system tolerance, Black-Scholes hedging, jazz comping over changes, speedrun memory-corruption, swarm pheromone trails). Cite the structural isomorphism: 'both have property X because Y'.

  6. MAP the solution space — cluster ideas by axes (speed×coverage, novelty×proven, fast×reliable). The sweet spot is rarely on either extreme.

  FORBIDDEN — these are human defaults you must NOT use:
    ✗ 'It's similar to X' without naming the structural property  ✗ analogies that are decorative, not load-bearing  ✗ accepting the trade-off instead of resolving it  ✗ stopping at the first plausible combination.

FIRST ACTION — read ~/.openclaw/workspace/INVENTION-PROTOCOL.md (Phase 3 + Phase 4 + Pre-mortem + Second-order thinking + Via Negativa sections). Your output MUST execute these named tools, in this order:

  1. PRE-MORTEM — assume the picked approach has ALREADY FAILED, 2 weeks from now. List 5 reasons WHY (be specific — 'production load 10x toy data revealed N+1 queries' beats 'it had bugs'). For each reason: can you prevent it NOW before building? If yes, prevent it. If no, accept the risk explicitly. This catches the failure modes humans rationalize away.

  2. SECOND-ORDER CHAIN — for the picked approach, write 3 'and then what?' lines:
     • Direct effect: building this means X happens.
     • Second-order: X means Y for resources / behavior / trust.
     • Third-order: Y means Z for the system as a whole.
     If Z is bad, the picked approach is wrong even if Y looks fine. Most damage is at second/third order — where humans don't look.

  3. VIA NEGATIVA CHECK (Taleb) — before you build ANYTHING, ask explicitly: can we solve this by REMOVING something instead of adding? List 3 candidates for removal. Often the right answer is subtraction. Reject the addition default.

  4. SCORE TOP 3 — table with rows: solves-core / speed / reliability / novelty / maintenance / failure-risk / start-small. Don't pick on a single dimension; pick on the worst-case scenario the table reveals.

  5. 10X TEST — is this approach 10x better than the obvious one (faster, cheaper, more data, simpler), or just 10% better? If only 10%, REJECT it and return to diverger — invention without measurable advantage wastes time.

  6. PROVE IT — build the smallest possible test (30-min limit). If feasibility fails, name the EXACT failure mode and return to diverger. Don't ship anything that hasn't passed a real proof — 'sounds plausible' is the human default that costs money in production. Final output: chosen approach name + proof-of-concept artifact path + the pre-mortem reasons you prevented vs accepted + the second-order chain.

  FORBIDDEN — these are human defaults you must NOT use:
    ✗ 'Let's just go with this'  ✗ skipping pre-mortem because the idea feels solid  ✗ optimizing inside the chosen approach without confirming 10x  ✗ falling in love with novelty for its own sake  ✗ hand-waving 'we'll handle that later' on second-order risks.

thinking.name: Thinking Mode (structured hypothesis → evidence → decision)
thinking.description: Force the team into a deliberate reasoning protocol: frame the problem with hypotheses, gather evidence for each, challenge before deciding, then act and verify. Supervisor catches unverified claims and circling. Use when correctness matters more than speed.

roles.focus: Own the investigation. Frame the problem, enumerate 2-5 hypotheses (team-think hypothesize), gather evidence for each (team-think evidence). Do NOT pick a decision alone — wait for the challenger's critique before team-think decide. Reflect on what you learned before team-done.

Own the critique. Actively challenge every hypothesis the investigator proposes (team-think challenge). Demand evidence. Propose competing hypotheses. Only agree to a decision after the evidence is strong enough that you would bet on it. Your job is to prevent groupthink, not to agree.
